theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What is a cornrow?
options: A braid made close to the scalp, picking up hair along a row
A single braid that hangs loose from one small square parting
A twist made from only two strands of hair, twisted together
A ponytail tied high at the crown with a band

questions.stem: How is a cornrow usually braided, so that it sits raised on the scalp?
options: By crossing the outer strands over the middle one (overhand)
By twisting two strands round and round each other
By tying a small knot in the hair at every section
By crossing the outer strands under the middle (underhand)

questions.stem: What are box braids?
options: Braids woven flat along the scalp in straight rows
Braids made only with yarn, never with hair
Single braids, each from its own square parting
Braids that are first made on a wig block and sewn in

questions.stem: What is a two-strand twist?
options: Three strands crossed under each other along the scalp
Two strands twisted round each other to the ends
One strand wound round a rod
Two braids joined at the nape

questions.stem: Why do many braiders use the feed-in method for cornrows with extensions?
options: It uses much more extension hair, so the braid looks fuller
It makes the braid very thick and heavy right at the start
It adds hair bit by bit, so there is less pull
It means that no partings are needed

questions.stem: Why do you check the length and strength of the client's natural hair before adding extensions?
options: Weak or short hair may not hold heavy extensions
Long hair never needs extensions
So that you can charge the client more for long hair
Extensions only work on hair that has been relaxed

questions.stem: During the consultation you see round, scaly bald patches on Kimone's scalp. What should you do?
options: Braid tightly over the patches so they are hidden
Rub gel into the patches first
Braid only the hair growing around the patches
Do not braid; advise her to see a doctor

questions.stem: You see head lice in a client's hair. Why should you not braid it?
options: Lice make the hair far too slippery to braid
Lice spread easily to other people and tools
Lice make the finished braids come loose fast
Lice are only a problem in very long hair

questions.stem: How should natural hair be detangled before braiding?
options: Gently, in sections, from the ends up to the roots
Quickly, with a fine-tooth comb, from the roots down
Dry, with a hard bristle brush all over the head
By pulling the knots apart hard with both hands

questions.stem: Why is natural hair often stretched (for example by blow-drying on low heat) before braiding?
options: It is easier to part and braid, with less pulling
It makes the natural hair grow longer under the braids
It stops the client feeling the braids
It means that the hair does not need to be washed first

questions.stem: Why should natural hair not be braided while it is soaking wet?
options: Wet hair will not hold a clean, straight parting
Wet hair makes the extension hair change colour
Water makes the finished braids far too loose
It shrinks as it dries and tightens the braids

questions.stem: What is traction alopecia?
options: Hair loss caused by a poor diet with no vegetables
Hair loss caused by colouring the hair too often
Hair loss caused by constant pulling on the hair
Hair loss that happens only in people of old age

questions.stem: Which sign shows that a braid is too tight?
options: The braid is smooth and even
Bumps, redness or pain at the braid's base
The client can move her head freely and is relaxed
The parting is straight and clean all along the row

questions.stem: The client says her new braids hurt at the edges. What should you do?
options: Tell her that the pain will stop in about a week
Give her a painkiller and finish the style
Loosen or redo those braids with less tension
Add more gel to the edges to calm them

questions.stem: Why should the hair at the edges (the front hairline) be braided with extra care?
options: It grows much faster than the rest of the hair
It is often fine and breaks easily
It needs heavier extensions
It is never seen at all once the hair is braided

questions.stem: Why should the weight of the extension hair suit the client's own hair?
options: Heavy extensions on weak hair can pull it out
Light extensions always fall out the same day
Heavy extensions make the braids last for years
Extension weight only matters for children

questions.stem: Some clients find that synthetic braiding hair makes the scalp itch. What can help?
options: Using twice as much extension hair on each braid
Rinsing it first, or using another type
Braiding the extensions much tighter at the root
Putting it under a hot dryer

questions.stem: How are the ends of synthetic braids usually sealed safely?
options: Burn them with a lighter while the client sits still
Glue them with nail glue
Dip them in hot water, away from the skin
Tie them very tightly with thin rubber bands

questions.stem: Which tool is used to make clean, straight partings for braids?
options: A wide-tooth comb
A paddle brush
A pick
A tail comb

questions.stem: Why are sectioning clips used during braiding?
options: To decorate the style
To hold the loose extension hair together
To stop the finished braids from unravelling
To hold back hair not being braided

questions.stem: Why should partings be clean and even in size?
options: So the style looks neat and balanced
So that the client cannot see any of her scalp
So that much less extension hair is needed
So that the braids can be taken out much faster

questions.stem: Before starting a cornrow design, what should you do?
options: Start braiding straight away and see how it turns out
Cut the client's hair to one length all over first
Plan and agree the pattern of the rows
Apply a relaxer so that the hair is easier to braid

questions.stem: Why should only a light amount of gel or braiding cream be used?
options: Too much builds up, flakes and attracts dirt
Gel makes the natural hair grow longer
Gel changes the colour of the extension hair
Light amounts make the braids much looser

questions.stem: How should combs and clips be dealt with between braiding clients?
options: Wiped on the client's towel and used again
Cleaned of hair, washed, then disinfected
Left in the client's hair for next time
Rinsed in water only

questions.stem: Why should the braider wash her hands before starting?
options: To remove germs that could pass on
To make the client's hair easier to grip
To help dry out the client's hair faster
To make the extension hair look shinier

questions.stem: What should happen to loose hair and extension pieces on the floor during a long braiding service?
options: Leave them on the floor until the end of the day
Push them under the chair
Sweep them up often to keep the area safe
Keep them to use on the next client

questions.stem: A braiding service may take many hours. How can you keep the client comfortable?
options: Ask her not to move or speak at all
Offer short breaks and a comfortable seat
Braid as fast as possible with high tension
Turn off the lights to help her rest

questions.stem: How can the braider avoid back and neck pain during long services?
options: Adjust the chair height and take short breaks
Bend low over the client for the whole service
Stand on one leg to stay alert
Braid with arms held high above the head

questions.stem: How do you keep a cornrow straight along its parting?
options: Pull hard on the braid so it cannot move
Braid with your eyes on the mirror only
Pick up hair from both sides of the parting line
Pick up hair evenly, only from its own section

questions.stem: Why should a braid be finished neatly at the end?
options: So that it can be cut off later more easily
Because loose ends grow faster
So the client cannot take it out
So it does not unravel and looks tidy

questions.stem: Why might a client with fragile natural hair be advised to have larger, fewer braids?
options: Larger braids always need a lot more extension hair
Very tiny braids on fragile hair can cause breakage
Larger braids take a lot longer to put in
Small braids can never be washed at all

questions.stem: When braiding a child's hair, what matters most?
options: Use heavy extensions so the style lasts longer
Braid as tightly as possible so it stays neat
Keep the tension low and the style light
Braid the edges very tightly

questions.stem: How should a client clean her scalp while wearing braids?
options: Never wash it at all until the braids are taken out
Scrub hard with a fine-tooth comb every single day
Cleanse gently, rinse well and dry fully
Pour plenty of oil over the scalp instead of washing it

questions.stem: Why should braids be dried fully after washing?
options: Damp braids make the hair grow faster
Dry braids are harder to take out
Wet braids change colour in the sun
Damp braids can smell and grow mildew

questions.stem: What should a client wear at night to protect her braids?
options: A satin or silk scarf or bonnet
A tight cotton hat
Nothing, so the scalp can breathe
A plastic shower cap with a hot towel

questions.stem: How long is it usually advised to keep braids in?
options: As long as possible, even a full year or more
A few weeks, often 6 to 8 at most
Only one day
Until the extensions fall out on their own

questions.stem: How should extension braids be taken out?
options: Pull each braid out quickly from the root
Cut each braid off very close to the scalp
Cut below the natural hair, then unbraid gently
Wash the braids first so that they slide out easily

questions.stem: After braids are taken out, a lot of loose hair comes away. Why?
options: The braids pulled all of that hair out at the root
The hair is falling out because of an illness
Hair that shed naturally was held in the braids
The comb broke the hair as it was removed

questions.stem: What should you check before the client leaves?
options: That she has paid for next month's visit as well
That all clips are still in her hair
That the braids are as tight as possible
That the braids are even, neat and comfortable

questions.stem: Why should you record the braid style, extension type and any reactions on the record card?
options: To plan the next visit and avoid problems
So that the client can be charged twice for it
Because the extension hair maker needs to know
To show the client's friends

questions.stem: Why must the hot water for sealing braid ends be handled with great care?
options: It makes the extension hair change colour
It cools the braids too quickly
It makes the scalp itch
It can scald the client or the braider

questions.stem: How should scissors be used when trimming extension ends?
options: Point them towards the client's face and neck
Cut away from the skin; close them after
Leave them open on the client's lap to save time
Carry them in your back pocket between cuts

questions.stem: Which product would you suggest for keeping natural hair under braids moisturised?
options: A thick wax rubbed onto the scalp daily
A strong clarifying shampoo every day
Hairspray on the roots every morning
A light leave-in spray or moisturiser

questions.stem: Why should you agree the style, size, length and price with the client before starting?
options: So that the client cannot leave before the end
So the client knows what to expect and is happy
So you can change the price later
So you can braid without stopping

questions.stem: A few days after braiding, a client comes back with painful, pus-filled bumps on her scalp. What should you do?
options: Rub plenty of gel onto the bumps to soothe them
Tell her that this is normal and send her home
Loosen the braids and refer her to a doctor
Re-braid the same area more tightly than before

How many strands of hair are used in a basic cornrow?
What is the name of the braid in which the outer strands cross over the middle, so that it lies flat and smooth?
What is the name of a twist made flat along the scalp, picking up hair as it goes?
What are braids called that start with the client's own hair and add extension hair little by little, with no knot at the root?
What is the name of the braid made from two sections, crossing small pieces from the outside of one section to the other?

For about how many minutes should a scald from hot water be cooled under cool running water?

essays.stem: Describe what you would discuss and check during a consultation before a braiding service.
essays.modelAnswer: I ask the client what style she wants, such as cornrows, box braids or twists, and show her pictures so that we agree on the size, length, pattern and colour. I ask whether she wants extensions and what type, and I check whether she has had an itch or a reaction to extension hair before. I ask about her lifestyle and how long she wants to keep the style. I look at her scalp for ringworm, lice, sores, cuts, bumps or thinning, especially at the edges; if I find any, I do not braid and advise her to see a doctor. I check her hair's length, density, elasticity and condition, to choose a braid size and extension weight that her hair can hold without damage. I explain how long the service will take, agree the price, give advice on comfort and breaks, and write it all on the record card.
markingPoints: Agrees the style, size, length, pattern and colour
Asks about extensions, past reactions and how long she will keep it
Checks the scalp and edges, and refers if there is a problem
Checks length, density, elasticity and condition to choose braid size and extension weight
Agrees time and price, and records everything

essays.stem: Describe how you would prepare natural hair for braiding, from shampoo to sectioning.
essays.modelAnswer: I check the scalp first. I shampoo the hair gently to remove dirt, oil and old product, then apply a moisturising conditioner. While the conditioner is in, I detangle the hair gently in sections with my fingers and a wide-tooth comb, starting at the ends and working up to the roots, so it does not break. I rinse and blot the hair with a towel. I apply a light leave-in conditioner. Then I stretch the hair, for example by blow-drying it on low or medium heat with a comb nozzle and a heat protectant, or by banding or twisting it, so it is easier to part and braid with less pulling. I do not braid soaking wet hair, because it shrinks as it dries and the braids get tight. When the hair is ready, I use a tail comb to part it into the main sections for the pattern, and hold them with clips.
markingPoints: Checks the scalp, then shampoos and conditions
Detangles gently from the ends to the roots
Applies a light leave-in or moisturiser
Stretches the hair (low-heat blow-dry with protectant, or banding) and does not braid it soaking wet
Parts into main sections with a tail comb and clips

essays.stem: Describe the steps for braiding one neat cornrow, with or without feed-in extensions.
essays.modelAnswer: I make a clean, straight parting with a tail comb on each side of the row, and clip the rest of the hair away. I apply a little braiding cream to smooth the hair. At the start of the row, I take a small piece of hair and divide it into three equal strands. I cross the outer strands under the middle strand in turn, which is an underhand braid, so that the braid sits raised on the scalp. Each time I cross a strand, I pick up a little hair from the row and add it to that strand, keeping the pieces even and only from inside the parting. For feed-in extensions, I add small amounts of extension hair little by little as I go, so the braid grows thicker gradually and does not pull at the start. I keep the tension firm but not tight. At the end of the row, I braid off the scalp and finish the end neatly.
markingPoints: Clean, straight partings with a tail comb; other hair clipped away
Divides into three even strands and crosses them under the middle (underhand)
Picks up even amounts of hair from inside the row only
Feeds in extension hair little by little to avoid pulling
Even, firm but not tight tension; finishes the end neatly

essays.stem: Describe how you would put in box braids with extensions and finish the ends safely.
essays.modelAnswer: After preparing and stretching the hair, I plan the size of the braids with the client and start at the nape. I take a square parting with a tail comb and clip the rest away. I choose an amount of extension hair that suits the client's own hair, so that it is not too heavy. I place the extension hair at the base of the section and divide the client's hair and the extension into three strands, then braid down evenly, keeping the tension firm but not tight and checking the base for pulling. I work up the head row by row, keeping the partings the same size. At the hairline, I use smaller amounts of extension and less tension. To seal synthetic ends, I follow the maker's instructions; often the ends are dipped in hot water from a heat-proof container, with a towel over the client's shoulders and the water kept well away from her skin. I never use a flame near the client.
markingPoints: Plans the size; square partings starting at the nape
Uses an extension weight that suits the client's hair
Braids evenly with firm but not tight tension, checking the base
Keeps partings even; takes extra care at the hairline
Seals ends as the maker says, using hot water safely; never a flame

essays.stem: Explain what traction alopecia is, what causes it, the signs to look for, and how a braider can prevent it.
essays.modelAnswer: Traction alopecia is hair loss caused by pulling on the hair for a long time. It often happens at the edges and temples, where the hair is finest. It is caused by braids that are too tight, extensions that are too heavy for the client's hair, very small braids on fragile hair, tight ponytails or buns, and keeping braids in for too long. Signs of too much tension are pain or a headache, redness, small bumps or spots at the base of the braids, the scalp pulled up into small peaks around a braid, and broken or thinning hair at the hairline. To prevent it, the braider should keep the tension firm but not tight, use extension weights that suit the hair, choose a suitable braid size, and take extra care at the edges. The client should not keep braids in too long. If a client feels pain, the braids should be loosened at once.
markingPoints: Hair loss caused by long-term pulling, often at the edges
Causes: tight braids, heavy extensions, tiny braids on fragile hair, keeping them in too long
Signs: pain, redness, bumps, scalp pulled into peaks, thinning edges
Prevention: low tension, suitable extension weight and braid size, care at the edges
Loosen braids that hurt; do not keep braids in too long

essays.stem: Describe how you would keep a braiding service hygienic, before, during and after it.
essays.modelAnswer: Before the service, I check the client's scalp, and I do not braid if there are lice, ringworm, sores or other infections; I advise her to see a doctor. I wash my hands, put a fresh towel, neck strip and cape on her, and lay out tools that have been cleaned and disinfected. I keep the extension hair in its packet until I need it, and keep it off the floor. During the service, I keep the work area tidy and sweep up loose hair and extension pieces often. If I drop a comb, I put it aside for cleaning and use a clean one. After the service, I throw away the neck strip and any loose hair, and put the towels in the laundry. I remove hair from the combs and clips, wash them in warm, soapy water, then disinfect them for the time the maker says, and dry and store them. I wipe the chair and trolley and wash my hands.
markingPoints: Checks the scalp and does not braid over infection (refers)
Washes hands; fresh towel, neck strip and cape; clean, disinfected tools
Keeps extensions clean and off the floor; sweeps up often; replaces dropped tools
Cleans then disinfects combs and clips as the maker says
Bins single-use items, launders towels, wipes surfaces, washes hands

essays.stem: Explain how you would choose extension hair for a braiding service.
essays.modelAnswer: I start with what the client wants: the style, the length, the colour and how long she will keep it. There are three main types. Synthetic braiding hair is cheaper and comes in many colours, and its ends can often be sealed with hot water as the maker says, but some clients find it makes the scalp itch. Human hair looks natural and can be washed and styled, but it costs more. Yarn is light and soft and is used for some braids and twists. I match the colour to the client's own hair or to the shade she wants. Most importantly, I make sure the weight and amount of extension suit the strength of her hair, because heavy extensions can pull weak hair out. If the client has itched before, I suggest rinsing the hair first, as the maker says, or another type. I read the packet for the fibre and the maker's instructions.
markingPoints: Starts from the style, length, colour and how long it will be kept
Describes synthetic, human hair and yarn and their features
Matches the colour to the client's hair or chosen shade
Chooses a weight and amount that the client's hair can hold
Deals with itching (rinse first or another type) and reads the maker's instructions

essays.stem: A braiding service can take many hours. Describe how you would keep the client and yourself safe and comfortable.
essays.modelAnswer: Before I start, I tell the client how long the service will take, and we agree on short breaks so that she can stretch, drink water and use the toilet. I seat her in a comfortable chair at a height that lets me work with a straight back, and I use a stool or adjust the chair as I move round her head. I take short breaks myself, stretch my hands and shoulders, and change position so that I do not strain my back and neck. I keep good lighting so that I can see the partings clearly. I keep the floor clear of loose hair and cords so that nobody slips or trips. I use scissors carefully, cutting away from the skin, and close them after each use. If I seal ends with hot water, I use a heat-proof container, keep it steady, and keep it away from the client's skin. I check often that the braids do not hurt.
markingPoints: Explains the time and agrees breaks for the client
Comfortable seat at the right height; braider keeps a straight back and changes position
Braider takes breaks and stretches; good lighting
Keeps the floor clear; uses scissors safely
Handles hot water safely and checks often that the braids do not hurt

essays.stem: What aftercare advice would you give a client with new braids, and why?
essays.modelAnswer: I would tell the client to cleanse her scalp gently every week or two with a diluted shampoo or a scalp cleanser, working it in with her fingertips, not her nails, then rinse well. She must dry the braids fully, because damp braids can smell and grow mildew. She should keep her scalp and hair moisturised with a light leave-in spray or moisturiser, but avoid heavy oils and too much gel, which build up and attract dirt. At night she should wear a satin or silk scarf or bonnet to reduce frizz and protect her edges. She should avoid tight buns and ponytails, especially in the first days. If she feels pain, sees bumps or redness, or the edges are thinning, she should come back so that the braids can be loosened. She should not keep the braids in too long, often about 6 to 8 weeks at most, and should book a removal appointment.
markingPoints: Cleanse the scalp gently and rinse well
Dry the braids fully to stop smell and mildew
Light moisturiser; avoid heavy oils and build-up
Satin or silk scarf at night; no tight buns or ponytails
Return if there is pain or bumps; do not keep braids in too long

essays.stem: Describe how to remove extension braids safely, and how to care for the hair afterwards.
essays.modelAnswer: I check the scalp and explain that some loose hair will come out, because the hair that sheds each day was held in the braids. I cut each braid carefully below the end of the client's natural hair, so that I do not cut her own hair. Then I unbraid each one gently from the end up to the root, using the end of a tail comb or my fingers. I spray a little water and leave-in conditioner to help, and I never pull the braid out from the root. When a braid is out, I gently remove the shed hair and any build-up at the base, working from the ends up. When all the braids are out, I shampoo the hair and scalp gently, then apply a deep conditioner, because the hair may be dry. I detangle again with a wide-tooth comb, from the ends up. I check the scalp and edges for damage and advise a rest before the next tight style.
markingPoints: Explains normal shedding; cuts below the natural hair end
Unbraids gently from the end to the root, never pulling
Uses water or leave-in to help; removes shed hair and build-up gently
Shampoos, deep-conditions and detangles from the ends
Checks the scalp and edges and advises a rest

practical1.title: Straight-back cornrows (cane rows) on natural hair
practical1.brief: As a group, braid a full head of straight-back cornrows on natural hair, on a model who agrees to it or on a practice head with natural textured hair. Share the work: one member leads the consultation, checks the scalp and edges, and fills in the record card; one shampoos, conditions and detangles the hair from the ends; one blow-dries it on low heat with a heat protectant to stretch it. Together, plan and agree the number of rows. Then each member parts and braids at least two rows from the front hairline to the nape while the assessor watches, using clean, straight partings, an underhand braid, and firm but not tight tension, with extra care at the edges. After each row, the member checks the base for pulling. Last, one member checks the whole head for even rows and comfort, and another gives aftercare advice. Photograph each stage below, showing the hair only, never the face unless the model agrees and the Centre allows it. Clean and disinfect the tools and hand in once for the whole group.
materials: A model who agrees, or a practice head with natural textured hair
Shampoo, moisturising conditioner and a light leave-in
Wide-tooth comb, tail combs and sectioning clips
Blow-dryer with a comb nozzle, and heat protectant
Disinfectant for combs and clips, as the Centre uses
photos: The hair detangled and stretched before braiding
The planned partings for the rows
A row being braided, showing the underhand braid and the parting
Close-up of the base of one row, showing no pulling or tenting
The finished cornrows from the top and back
The tools in the disinfectant and the area swept
checklist: Checked the scalp and edges before starting
Detangled the hair gently from the ends upwards
Made clean, straight partings of even size
Braided underhand with even pick-ups from the row only
Kept the tension firm but not tight, with extra care at the edges
Finished each row neatly and checked the base for pulling
Cleaned and disinfected tools and left the area tidy
safety: Do not braid over lice, ringworm, sores or open cuts; refer to a doctor
Keep tension low enough that the client feels no pain, and loosen any braid that hurts
Sweep up loose hair often so nobody slips
Give the client breaks and keep a good working posture

practical2.title: Box braids with extensions, with the ends sealed safely
practical2.brief: As a group, put in individual box braids with extension hair on a practice head with natural hair, or on a model who agrees to it (a model may have a partial head done to keep the time reasonable). Share the work: one member leads the consultation and chooses the extension type, colour and weight with the group, writing the reasons on the record card; one prepares and stretches the hair; one divides the head into sections with clean partings. Then each member puts in at least six box braids while the assessor watches, starting at the nape, with square partings of even size, the right amount of extension, and firm but not tight tension. One member takes extra care with smaller braids at the hairline. Last, with the instructor present, one member seals the synthetic ends as the maker says, using hot water from a heat-proof container, with a towel over the shoulders and the water kept away from the skin. Never use a flame. Photograph each stage below, showing the hair only, never the face unless the model agrees and the Centre allows it. Clean up and hand in once for the whole group.
materials: A practice head with natural hair, or a model who agrees
Synthetic braiding hair (or yarn) chosen with the group
Tail combs, wide-tooth comb and sectioning clips
Braiding cream or light gel and a light leave-in
Heat-proof container and hot water, used only with the instructor present
Disinfectant for combs and clips, as the Centre uses
photos: The record card showing the extension type, colour and weight chosen
The square partings at the nape before braiding
Extension hair being added at the base of a braid
A row of finished box braids, showing even partings
The smaller braids at the hairline
The ends being sealed safely in hot water, with a towel over the shoulders
The finished style from the back, and the area cleaned
checklist: Helped choose an extension weight that suits the client's hair
Made square partings of even size
Added the extension neatly at the base without bulk or pulling
Braided evenly to the ends with firm but not tight tension
Took extra care and used less tension at the hairline
Sealed or finished the ends safely as the maker says, with no flame
Used scissors safely, cutting away from the skin
Cleaned and disinfected tools and swept up loose hair
safety: Seal ends only with the instructor present, keeping hot water away from skin; never use a flame
Keep tension low enough that the client feels no pain; loosen any braid that hurts
Cut away from the skin and close scissors after each use
Sweep up loose hair and extension pieces often so nobody slips
Give the client breaks during the long service
